Citi's card business is growing: Third-quarter card spending rose 11% and loans increased 6%, with 86% of card customers having FICO scores of 660 or higher. The bank said customers are borrowing and spending in a disciplined way.

Citi is investing in card products, customer acquisition and loyalty to pursue mid-single-digit revenue and loan growth; its U.S. card business serves 70 million consumers and is near its target of low-20s returns on tangible common equity through the cycle.

AI is a growing focus: Citi is applying it to fraud detection, cybersecurity and marketing, while preparing conversational tools for tasks such as booking travel with rewards and working to keep AI-assisted card transactions secure.

Bonds Are Paying 5% Again, and the Repricing Has Reached Every Corner of the Market

Citigroup (NYSE:C) is investing in credit card products, customer acquisition and artificial intelligence as it targets growth in its U.S. card business, while seeing continued resilience among its largely prime customer base, an executive said at a fintech conference.

Pam Habner, head of U.S. Consumer Cards at Citi, said third-quarter card spending rose 11% and loans grew 6%. She cautioned that the bank's customer base does not represent every segment of the U.S. consumer: 86% of its card customers have FICO scores of 660 or higher.

Habner said experts generally expected holiday spending growth of about 5%, while noting that the outcome remained to be seen. She also pointed to a gap between consumer sentiment and behavior, saying consumers have remained pessimistic even as they continue to spend.

Habner said Citi is increasing investment in products, customer acquisition and loyalty benefits while seeking efficiencies to fund growth. The business has an efficiency ratio of about 37%, she said. Acquiring card customers can take three to five years to pay back, making it a longer-term investment than some automation projects.

title: Goldman, Citi and Other Banks Reportedly Fund $270 Million Stablecoin Initiative
detail:
Goldman, Citi and Other Banks Reportedly Fund $270 Million Stablecoin Initiative
Goldman, Citi and other banks reportedly commit $270 million to Project Faro
Unchained
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 1:20 PM MST 2 min read
GS
C
SAN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stablecoin venture that 21 financial firms unveiled in September has about $270 million in commitments from its backers, with Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Banco Santander and Deutsche Bank among the banks putting up money, according to a report on Tuesday that cited people familiar with the matter.

The funding is meant to pay for the planned issuer's first five years, the report said. Its backers plan to incorporate the issuer, codenamed Project Faro, in the U.S. and are still looking for a chief executive, according to the report.

Versions of the report published by other outlets did not say whether the money is equity or another form of capital, how much each bank is putting in, or which blockchain the token will use. No bank or the venture has commented publicly on the report.

Get Unchained's crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.

Two Issuers Hold Most of the Supply

The group's first token will be pegged to the U.S. dollar, a market where two issuers account for most of the supply. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC made up about 84% of the roughly $293 billion in dollar-pegged stablecoins in circulation on Tuesday, Unchained calculated from DefiLlama's stablecoin data. USDT had about $176 billion outstanding and USDC about $70 billion.

What the Group Announced in September

The 21 firms said on Sept. 1 that they would set up a new company in the second half of 2026, subject to closing conditions, to issue a stablecoin, and Unchained reported on the plan that day. A dollar token comes first, with a longer-term aim of expanding to other Group of Seven (G7) currencies, a euro version being the priority. The group is targeting the first half of 2027 to go to market.

Besides the four lenders the report named as committing the money, members include Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Fidelity Investments, BBVA, Lloyds Banking Group and MUFG Bank. The effort grew out of a group of 10 banks that said in October 2025 it was exploring a reserve-backed form of digital money.

The group said it intends to comply with the U.S. Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act and the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation, "as applicable." The Sept. 1 announcement said the company's name would be announced later.

The group also faces other bank and corporate token efforts, some involving the same banks. JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America and Wells Fargo plan a tokenized deposit network, which would put customer bank deposits on a blockchain, for 2027, while the Open USD stablecoin, whose backers include Coinbase, Visa and Stripe, already has about $924 million in circulation, according to DefiLlama.

title: Goldman, Citi and Global Banks Commit $270 Million to Challenge Crypto’s Stablecoin Giants
detail:
Goldman, Citi and Global Banks Commit $270 Million to Challenge Crypto’s Stablecoin Giants
Decrypt Staff
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 11:33 AM MST 3 min read
GS
C
SAN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The group of global banks building a joint stablecoin has put real money on the table, committing around $270 million to fund the venture as it moves from blueprint to buildout.

Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Banco Santander, and Deutsche Bank are among the institutions backing the effort, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The capital is meant to cover five years of operations for a planned U.S.-incorporated company that will issue a dollar-denominated stablecoin. Known among participants as Project Faro, the venture is still searching for a chief executive, and its final name remains under discussion.

A spokesperson for the project declined to comment, as did Santander and Deutsche Bank, while Goldman and Citi referred questions to the project.

The funding is the concrete next step for an initiative that first went public late last year. As Decrypt previously reported, 21 of the world's largest financial institutions committed in September to form a company to issue a U.S. dollar stablecoin, targeting a launch in the first half of 2027, with a euro version and other currencies to follow.

That consortium had more than doubled from an initial group of 10 banks that began exploring the idea in October 2025, and now spans North America, Europe, East Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

Beyond the four named by Bloomberg, its participants include Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Fidelity Investments, PNC, Capital One, TD Bank, UBS, BBVA, Deutsche Bank, Lloyds Banking Group and MUFG, among others. JPMorgan, notably, is not on the list.

The venture is one of several collaborative pushes by established finance into a business long dominated by crypto-native players. Visa, Mastercard and Stripe are among more than 100 companies backing the issuer Open Standard, while European banks have formed Qivalis to issue a euro-denominated coin.

At the moment, Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC together account for about 85% of a market worth roughly $290 billion, nearly all of it dollar-pegged. When the bank consortium first went public in September, Circle's stock fell about 6% as investors priced in the prospect of bank-backed competition for USDC.

The banks are betting that institutional trust, regulatory alignment and existing client networks can win them a share of a settlement business that promises round-the-clock, cross-border payments at lower cost than traditional rails.

Wall Street's Plumbing Goes Onchain as Morgan Stanley Tokenizes Securities

The token is being designed to comply with the U.S. GENIUS Act, which created the first federal framework for dollar-pegged tokens in 2025, and, where applicable, the EU's MiCA regime. The group has said it wants the stablecoin used across wholesale, institutional and retail markets.

The injection formalizes an ambitious initiative detailed in September by 21 international institutions seeking to counter crypto-native incumbents through institutional-grade digital settlement assets. While the venture initially aims to issue a dollar-pegged token, the consortium plans to subsequently expand issuance into other G7 currencies, prioritizing a euro offering. Regulatory tailwinds have increasingly catalyzed traditional finance's push into digital assets, supported by federal legislation enacted in 2025 to create a defined legal perimeter for reserve-backed payment tokens. title: A $13 Billion Fund Dumps These 3 Stocks
detail:
A $13 Billion Fund Dumps These 3 Stocks
Roxanna Maglangit
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 9:51 AM MST 6 min read
JPM
C
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
A $13 Billion Fund Dumps These 3 Stocks ©@baramee2554 from Getty Images Pro via Canva
Key Takeaways

A $13 billion fund, MKP Capital Management, sold all of its JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Microsoft shares in the third quarter.

JPMorgan was the largest of the three exits, at 12.8% of the fund's 13F stocks on June 30.

Wall Street's average targets sit 6% above JPMorgan's last close, 14% above Microsoft's and 21% above Citigroup's.

The numbers back the JPMorgan sale best, and Citigroup is the one of the three worth buying back.

A $13 billion fund just walked away from JPMorgan Chase (JPM:NYSE), Citigroup (C:NYSE) and Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ).

MKP Capital Management, which manages $12.85 billion in all, held none of the three on Sept. 30. That's according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 4, which lists $3.26 billion of US stocks in 20 positions.

Two banks and Microsoft, gone

Three months earlier, these were real positions: JPMorgan alone was 12.8% of the fund's 13F stocks, Citigroup 3.6% and Microsoft 3.5%.

The fund still holds a bank. By Sept. 30, Goldman Sachs was its third-largest position, at 8.9% of its 13F stocks, after the fund raised its share count 176%. Apple was a new position at 5.0%.

A 13F shows only what a fund held on the last day of the quarter. It doesn't say when the fund sold, at what price, or why. It also leaves out shorts, bonds, cash and stocks listed outside the US, and that matters for a firm whose US stocks come to $3.26 billion of the $12.85 billion it manages.

Each stock's move below runs from June 30, the last quarter-end when the fund held it, to the latest close. It says nothing about what the fund got for its shares.

JPMorgan's exit has the numbers on its side

On June 30, the fund held 1.42 million JPMorgan shares worth $466 million. The stock is up 8% since then.

The third quarter brought JPMorgan's first earnings miss in nearly three years: EPS of $5.57 against a consensus near $5.90, as expenses rose 12%. The bank still raised its 2026 net interest income outlook to about $97.2 billion excluding Markets. It also earned 20% on tangible common equity, above its 17% through-the-cycle target. But net buybacks fell to $664 million in the quarter, and management now puts its excess capital at about $30 billion, down from at least $60 billion in May 2025.
